Continuity of a function, types of discontinuity, graphs of discontinuous function
Derivatives: derivative of a function, derivatives of algebraic, trigonometric, inverse trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions by definition (simple forms)
Rules of differentiation; derivatives of parametric and implicit functions; higher order derivatives
Geometric interpretation of derivative; monotonicity of a function, interval of monotonicity, extreme values of a function, concavity, points of inflection
Anti-derivatives: integration using basic integrals, integration by substitution and by parts methods
The definite integral; the definite integral as an area under the given curve; area between two curves

card.title: Limits: Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential and Logarithmic

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Three standard limits — the sine, tangent and cosine forms — unlock most of the topic, and all assume radians, which is the trap that changes every numerical answer. Rational functions and compositions of continuous functions settle themselves by direct substitution.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Using the standard limits with x in degrees, which changes every value by a factor involving $\pi$.  ·  Applying $\lim \ln f = \ln(\lim f)$ when the limit of $f$ is negative, where the logarithm is not defined at all.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Where a formula is quoted it is valid only under the conditions stated; Using the standard limits with x in degrees, which changes every value by a factor involving $\pi$.  ·  Every result here follows from the definitions, so a first-principles derivation is always a valid fallback in the exam.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: All three standard trigonometric limits assume radians.  ·  Continuous functions compose, so most limits need no special technique.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Forgetting that the $1^\infty$ case needs logarithms and cannot be handled by L'Hôpital directly.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Work through the authored practice problems and re-derive each key formula from the definition.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Switch the calculator to radians before evaluating anything in this topic.  ·  If the answer involves $\frac{\pi}{180}$, the degrees/radians conversion was missed.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Combining a standard limit with a substitution such as $u=3x$ is a reliable 2–3 mark question.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Topic anchor: Composition of continuous functions settles most limits if $f$ is continuous at $a$ and $g$ is continuous at $f(a)$, then $ lim_{x to a}g(f(x))=g(f(a))$.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: $1^\infty$ limits are handled by taking logarithms first.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The limit defining $e$ is exactly the $1^\infty$ case, which is why $e$ governs continuous compounding rather than discrete interest steps.  ·  In physics, $\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}=1$ is why the small-angle approximation $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ is valid for pendulum and projectile work — and it only holds in radians.

rows.text: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}$ (radians) is: → B  ·  The standard limit $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ holds when $x$ is measured in: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **The standard limits that unlock everything else:** $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$, $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x}{x}=1$, and $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\frac12$. The second follows from the first and the third from the half-angle identity, so only one needs proving.  ·  **All three assume RADIANS.** In degrees each is scaled: $\lim\frac{\sin x}{x}=\frac{\pi}{180}$ and $\lim\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{360}$. A calculator left in degree mode produces exactly the wrong value, which is the most practical trap in the topic.  ·  **Rational functions and polynomials substitute directly:** since polynomials are continuous everywhere and rational functions are continuous away from their zeros, $\lim_{x\to a}\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}=\frac{P(a)}{Q(a)}$ whenever $Q(a)\ne0$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Rational: $\lim_{x\to a}\frac{P}{Q}=\frac{P(a)}{Q(a)}$ for $Q(a)\ne0$  ·  $\lim_{x\to a}e^{f}=e^{f(a)}$, $\lim_{x\to a}\ln f=\ln f(a)$ for $f(a)>0$  ·  Statement 1: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ for $x$ in radians.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 2: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\frac12$.  ·  Statement 3: For $Q(a)\ne0$, $\lim_{x\to a}\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}=\frac{P(a)}{Q(a)}$.  ·  Statement 4: $\lim_{x\to a}\ln f(x)=\ln f(a)$ requires $f(a)>0$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 5: $\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+\frac1n)^n=e$.  ·  **Exponential and logarithmic limits are continuous functions:** $\lim_{x\to a}e^{f(x)}=e^{f(a)}$ and $\lim_{x\to a}\ln f(x)=\ln f(a)$ for $f(a)>0$. The domain condition on the logarithm is what excludes $f(a)\le0$.  ·  **The $1^\infty$ family via logarithms:** for $y=(1+\frac{1}{x})^x$, take logs to get $\lim x\ln(1+\frac1x)$, a $0/0$ form, and L'Hôpital then gives $\lim\frac{\frac{1}{x}cdot rac{1}{1+1/x}}{1}=1$, so the limit is $e$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Composition of continuous functions settles most limits:** if $f$ is continuous at $a$ and $g$ is continuous at $f(a)$, then $\lim_{x\to a}g(f(x))=g(f(a))$. This is why almost no work is needed for expressions built from polynomials, roots, exponentials and logarithms with well-behaved arguments.
